targets.text: culture-agents runs a small fleet without losing track of work: two runs can work in one repository at once, a restarted core takes back live control of the workers that survived it, a duplicate submit is answered once, work is placed only on a host that can take it, a halted host is never reported as a success, and a question a run asks its operator is still waiting after a restart.
Every clause of the announcement is covered by a requirement in this frame and by a test in the D2 acceptance suite; a clause without a passing test is reported as not delivered.

Operators and calling agents (the agents CLI today; culture-rules and embodiment later) that submit work to more than one culture-agents host and need the state they read to stay true across restarts and host failures.
The agents CLI is the only caller D2 is tested with. culture-rules and embodiment are named as later callers and nothing in D2 is built for them alone.

After a core restart, the core takes back live control (steer, cancel, attach) of every worker that survived it. reconcile() rebuilds the in-memory controls map through the existing reconnectWorker, and the 'reconnect' capability stops being refused.

Reattach is proven by killing the core process (SIGKILL, not a clean stop) while a stub-harness run is mid-turn, starting a new core, and observing a steer and a cancel take effect on that run. A worker whose control socket no longer answers is reported 'unknown', never reattached by guess.

Two or more runs can be active in one repository at the same time, each steered independently. No limit applies unless the operator configures one; a configured limit is a check at submit. The one-active-run-per-repository 'busy' rule is removed, and the 'worktree_isolation' capability reports what is actually guaranteed.

Two concurrent runs in one repository each return commits only on their own `runs/<id>` branch, and neither branch contains the other's commits. The bound is a number a caller can read, and a submit past it gets a typed refusal, not a queue that is silently created.

Per-run isolation stays what D1 built: each run works in its own sandbox clone made from a git bundle, and its commits return into its own `runs/<id>` branch. The host checkout and index are never written, and no git worktree is created on the host.
No code path in D2 calls 'git worktree' or writes the host checkout or index. This holds only if q1 is answered 'sandbox clones are the isolation D2 means'.

A duplicate submit with the same idempotency key returns the first run instead of starting a second one, and the same key with a different request is refused as a conflict. Steer and cancel deduplicate on their keys the same way. The key index is on disk, so it holds across a restart.

The key index is written to disk before the submit is acknowledged, so a crash between the two cannot produce a second run for the same key. The comparison that decides 'same request' is stated in the contract, including how long a key is remembered.

A run can ask its operator a question and wait. The question is written to the run's on-disk log, is still pending after a core restart, and 'agents runs answer' delivers the answer into the same run. A harness that cannot ask says so in its capability report.

At least one real harness can ask and wait without allow-all approvals. docs/d0/probe.md:286-295 lists approvals as unverified in the AI SDK adapter, so this requirement is conditional on a probe that runs before the plan; if no harness can ask, the capability is reported unsupported and the requirement is cut down to the store and the 'answer' verb against the stub.

A submit names where the work may run, and the core admits it only when that host can take it: the harness is available, a configured limit has room, and the host's heat signal does not say hold. The model-gateway signal joins the check for harnesses that use the gateway once lobes publishes an admit field with a timestamp; D2 ships without waiting for it. A signal that is missing or stale reads as unknown: a remote submit is refused and a local one is admitted with a warning. An unknown signal is never a hard failure of the control plane.

The heat signal is read as heat-governor publishes it, with no change there. The gateway signal is read only from the admit field that the lobes issue adds; until a lobes release has it, the gateway signal is not consulted and the capability report says so.

When a host halts or cannot be reached, every run that was active on it reads 'unreachable' to every caller, and never 'succeeded'. 'unreachable' is a view, not a stored state: the stored terminal state 'unknown' is still written only by the owning core, as on one host.

A halted host is detected by something that can be tested (a missed heartbeat or a failed request with a stated timeout), and the reader's answer never changes a run's stored terminal state: 'unknown' is a view until the host returns and reports.

Finished runs stop accumulating: there is a way to list the `runs/<id>` branches a repository holds, and a rule for removing one that requires positive evidence its commits are kept elsewhere (merged, or on another ref). Unknown liveness defers removal; nothing is force-deleted.

Removal never runs 'git branch -D'. The evidence rule (merged into a named ref, or reachable from another ref) is checked by git itself, and a branch whose run is 'unknown' or still retained is skipped and listed as skipped.

The three recovery gaps recorded after D1 are closed: a cancel whose grace period ends during retention cleanup still leaves a retention record, the worker's 'conflict' reply on a refused append has a test, and the daemon installs its signal handlers before it reports that it is listening.

Each of the three gaps has a test that fails on today's main and passes after the fix: late cancel during retention cleanup still leaves a retention record; the worker's 'conflict' reply; signal handlers installed before the 'listening' log line (core/src/daemon/main.ts:135-139).

The contract keeps its D1 guarantees: no AI SDK type appears in it, an unsupported action is refused with the typed 'unsupported' error naming the capability, the event cursor stays per run, gapless and never reset, a terminal state is final, and 'unknown' is never reported as success.
The contract tests that hold these guarantees in D1 still pass unchanged in meaning under API 3.0; a guarantee that 3.0 must weaken is listed in the spec as a breaking change, not changed silently.

Workers stay detached processes that never depend on the core: a core stop or crash never signals them, each one enforces its own deadline and writes its own terminal event, and the per-run control socket protocol does not change.
A test stops and kills the core while runs are active and asserts that no worker received a signal and each run still reached its own terminal event or deadline.

Local use keeps its D1 security posture: the owner-only Unix socket, deny by default dispatch, and an exact-match allow-list that no API route can read or write. A network transport is added beside the socket, not in place of it.
With no network transport configured, the core opens no listening TCP socket (checked in a test), and the allow-list file is not reachable through any route, new or old.

After part one, on one host: a core that restarts steers, cancels and attaches to the workers that outlived it; one repository holds several active runs up to a stated bound; a repeated submit, steer or cancel with the same idempotency key takes effect once; a run's question to its operator is on disk and answerable after a restart; finished run branches can be listed and removed with evidence. After part two: the same control API is reachable on more than one host, a submit is admitted only where the host can take it, and a run on a halted host reads 'unknown'.
Each sentence of the after state maps to one requirement (c3, c4, c6, c7, c8, c9, c10); the part-two half is not claimed as delivered when only part one has shipped.

Today (D1, control API 2.0), a restarted core reads a surviving worker's state from disk but cannot steer, cancel or attach to it: reconnectWorker exists (core/src/worker/spawn.ts:201) and only tests call it. A second submit to a repository with an active run is refused as busy (core/src/runs/service.ts:117-129). The idempotency key is stored on the run (core/src/runs/service.ts:141) and never compared. 'answer' is always refused as unsupported (contract/api.json:477-480). The API is served on one Unix socket on one host. Nothing lists or removes `runs/<id>` branches.
Every file and line cited in the before state is re-read on main when the spec is exported, and a citation that has moved is corrected before export.

Issue #2 allows archiving agent-lifecycle and cultureagent only after this repository passes recovery tests, and D3 to D5 (chat, culture-rules, embodiment) will submit work to it without a person watching. A caller that retries after a timeout, or reads state after a restart, has to get a true answer: one run, not two, and never a success the core did not observe.
The recovery tests issue #2 requires before archiving agent-lifecycle and cultureagent are named in the spec, and D2 states which of them it passes and which it leaves for D6.

Part one passes a D2 acceptance suite in tests/acceptance/d2/ with a mock stage that always runs: (1) kill the core with 2 runs active in 1 repository, restart it, then steer one and cancel the other, and both take effect; (2) send the same submit 2 times with 1 idempotency key and count exactly 1 run, and the same key with a different request returns 'conflict'; (3) a run asks a question, the core restarts, the question is still pending, and 'agents runs answer' delivers it; (4) a submit past the concurrency bound is refused with a typed error; (5) 0 runs report 'succeeded' unless a worker wrote that terminal event.
The mock stage uses the real CLI and the real core with the stub harness, as the D1 suite does, and a live stage reports NOT VERIFIED when a harness is unavailable, never a pass.

Part two passes on at least 2 real hosts: a submit from host A runs on host B and is steered and cancelled from A; with host B halted, every run that was active on it reads 'unknown' on A within a stated number of seconds and 0 read 'succeeded'; a submit to a host whose heat or gateway signal says hold is refused, and a missing signal reads 'unknown'.
The two hosts are mesh members that announced themselves. The acceptance record names them by role (host A, host B), never by host name; this replaces h19's 'named by the owner'.

A core announces itself as a fleet member when it starts and stops being listed when it stops or goes silent. Callers discover members from those announcements; no list of hosts is kept in the repository or in a tracked file.

A test starts two cores, sees each list the other after its announcement, stops one, and sees it leave the list within a stated number of seconds while its active runs read 'unknown' (c9), not removed.

No real host list, address or network detail of the fleet appears in a tracked file, a test fixture or a published record. Fixtures, documents and tests use one example node, a Jetson Thor, in place of 'spark'; acceptance records name real hosts by role (host A, host B).
Tracked files name only the example node; no real host list or network address of the fleet appears in one. The rename from 'spark' covers the contract fixtures.

Every run event the core appends to a run's log is also published to the existing broker (events-cli), in the envelope that broker's consumers already read. Publishing is best effort and comes after the on-disk append: the log stays the source of truth, a subscriber that missed events catches up from the log by cursor, and a broker that is down or slow never blocks, fails or delays a run.

A test runs a run to completion with the broker stopped and gets the same terminal state and the same event log as with the broker up; a second test subscribes, drops the connection mid-run, and recovers every missed event from the log by cursor with no duplicate.

Each run records who submitted it, as the core established it and never from a request field: for a local call, the user that owns the control socket; for a call from another host, the authenticated fleet member. The field is in the run's contract shape. Part one does not enforce on it; part two's ownership rules read it.
No request field can set or change the submitter; for a local call it equals the user that owns the socket, for a remote call the member the connection authenticated as. This replaces h24.

Local callers are authenticated by the operating system through file permissions: the control socket is owner-only (mode 0600 in a 0700 directory), so only the user that runs the core can connect, and no password or token is used locally. Reading the peer user of each connection is not part of D2.
A test connects as a different operating-system user and is refused by the file system, before the core sees a request; the socket and its directory keep modes 0600 and 0700. This replaces h25.

Cores on different hosts authenticate each other with key pairs, not a shared secret: each core has its own private key, peers hold only its public key, and the connection between two cores is encrypted and mutually authenticated. No secret that grants membership is ever sent over the network, and one host's key gives no access as any other host.

A test shows a core with an unknown key is refused, a core whose key was removed from a peer's trust list is refused on its next connection, and a packet capture of a join contains no private key and no reusable secret. The private key reaches the daemon through grant at start and is not written to a tracked file, a log or an event.

Fleet membership does not travel over the chat mesh. The mesh's link password is neither reused nor read by culture-agents, and a stopped chat server changes nothing about which hosts are members or whether a run can be controlled.
The D2 part-two acceptance run passes with no chat server running on either host, and no code in core/ opens a connection to an IRC port or reads the mesh's link secrets.

A remote submit names the repository as the executing host knows it (that host's allow-listed path, or an alias the host defines), and a run's commits can be fetched from the executing core through the control API as a git bundle, so a caller on another host can bring the `runs/<id>` branch home without shell access to that host.

A test submits from host A to host B, fetches the result bundle through the API on A and verifies it with 'git bundle verify'; the bundle route serves only refs under `runs/<id>` of a run the caller may read.

Two fleet members never share a node name: an announcement from a core whose node name is already held by a different key is refused and reported. Run ids stay `<node>-<agent>.run.<ULID>`, so the node part of any run id names the host that owns it.
A test starts a second core with the first one's node name and a different key and sees its announcement refused; no run id minted by one member can be minted by another.

Each member's capability report states its configured limits (or that none is set), how many runs are active, and its admission state per signal (admit, hold or unknown), so a caller that must choose a host can do so from the API. The caller chooses the host; D2 has no scheduler.
The fields are in contract/capabilities.json and a test reads them from two members; the report never shows another host's data.

A deadline sent to another host is evaluated on the executing core's clock from a duration, not from the caller's absolute time, and ordering across hosts never relies on comparing two hosts' clocks. Order within a run stays the cursor.
A test submits with the caller's clock set several minutes off and the run gets the full requested duration; no code compares a timestamp from one host with a clock on another.

The agents CLI sends an idempotency key on every submit, steer and cancel (generated when the user gives none) and, after a timeout, retries with the same key instead of telling the user to retry by hand.
A test drops the response of a submit and sees the CLI's retry return the first run; the 'unavailable' hint no longer suggests a bare retry for a request that may have been accepted.
The core removes its fleet private key and every other injected secret from the environment before it spawns a worker or runs a host command; no worker, sandbox or harness process can read them.

A test starts the core with a marker secret injected, submits a run and shows the marker is absent from the worker's environment and from the sandbox. Today a worker inherits process.env (core/src/worker/spawn.ts:168) and host commands filter only GIT_*, GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and SSH_AUTH_SOCK (core/src/sandbox/host-command.ts:29-39).

Events published to the broker carry lifecycle facts only: run id, event type, state, cursor and time. They never carry prompt text, harness output, tool results or an operator's answer. A subscriber that wants content reads it from the core by cursor, under the core's own access rules.

A test publishes a run whose output contains a marker string and shows the marker in no broker message. The broker accepts anonymous local subscribers (events-cli mosquitto.conf:49-61), while run logs on disk are mode 0600 because 'harness output may contain secrets' (core/src/store/files.ts:1-4).

Published run events use a type prefix of their own with at most four segments (for example agents.run.finished), an id derived from the run id and cursor so a republished event has the same id, and the run's cursor in the envelope so a consumer can resume from the log.

culture-rules subscribes to every type of up to four segments and already owns rules.run.* (culture_rules/events/emit.py:80, events_cli_adapter.py:58-66); a test publishes each run event type and reads it back through an events-cli subscriber, and publishing the same event twice yields one id.

A caller that cannot reach a member shows that member's runs as 'unreachable', a view that is never stored. The terminal state 'unknown' is written only by the core that owns the run, when it has evidence that the worker is gone. A run shown as unreachable can still end in any terminal state once its host answers.
A test partitions two hosts while a run is active, sees 'unreachable' on the caller, heals the partition and sees the run's real terminal state; no terminal state was written by the caller's side.

Two cores on different minor versions of the same API major can call each other in both directions; the version rule for core-to-core calls is stated in the contract, and a rolling upgrade of the fleet never needs all hosts to change at once.

Today's rule is 'same major and server minor at least the client minor' (contract/README.md:91-92), which fails in one direction between two cores at different minors; a test runs a 3.0 core against a 3.1 core in both directions.

A restarted core finishes reattaching before it answers control requests for a run: until a run's reattach attempt has completed, a steer, cancel or attach for it waits or is answered 'retry shortly', never 'live control unavailable'. Controls of runs that are already terminal are not rebuilt.

Today the daemon listens before reconcile() runs (core/src/daemon/main.ts:113 against :120) and each reattach can take up to 1 second (core/src/worker/spawn.ts:201); a test sends a steer in the first second after a restart with several live runs and it takes effect.

A submit that was in flight when the core died is accounted for after the restart: its worker, if one was spawned, appears as a run, and a repeat of the same idempotency key returns that run. The order on disk is key first, then the run directory, then the spawn; a key whose run was never established is released, and run directories without a first event and leftover temporary files are removed at startup.

A test kills the core at each step of a submit (after the key, after the run directory, after the spawn) and after restart finds exactly one run or none for that key, never two and never a key that answers 'not found'. Today a failed spawn leaves its directory behind, a directory without event 1 is invisible and never cleaned (core/src/store/derive.ts:67-71), and crash-left temporary files are never removed.

A run's base commit is resolved when the submit is accepted and is written on the run record. Concurrent runs in one repository each start from the commit recorded for them, not from wherever the operator's HEAD is when their sandbox becomes ready.

Today the base is the host's HEAD resolved inside the worker after the sandbox is ready, up to 180 seconds after the submit, and is recorded nowhere durable (core/src/sandbox/worktree.ts:112, core/src/sandbox/run-sandboxes.ts:165, core/src/worker/run-loop.ts:210). A test moves HEAD between submit and sandbox start and the run still starts from the recorded commit; the branch-removal evidence rule (c10) reads the recorded base.

The operator can configure a limit on concurrent runs per repository and per host; none applies by default. A configured limit is checked when the submit is accepted, and a submit past it is refused with a typed error naming the limit. A host that cannot take a run for lack of capacity refuses at submit where it can know, and otherwise fails the run with a reason that names the capacity.

With no limit configured no submit is refused for a limit; with one configured, a test sees the typed refusal at the limit. Today no bound exists and a gateway out of capacity shows up after the submit was acknowledged (core/src/harness/common/run-driver.ts:240-243).
With 2 runs active in 1 repository, a third submit to another repository returns its run id in under 2 seconds, and a cancel reaches 'cancelled' in under 10 seconds on both harnesses.

All submits are serialised today and each can wait up to 10 seconds for its worker (core/src/runs/service.ts:63-64, core/src/worker/spawn.ts:181), and OpenCode's cancel already takes 8.6 to 8.9 seconds of the 10 allowed with one run (docs/d0/d1-acceptance.md:167). The live stage measures both under concurrency; a miss is reported, not waived.

The run store carries a schema version. A 3.0 core reads run directories written by a 2.0 core and shows those runs; it never treats a record it cannot read as absent, and a run it cannot read never keeps a repository busy for ever. The upgrade procedure is stated: whether active 2.0 workers must finish first, and what the core does if they have not.

Today there is no store version, records and events are strictly validated, a new required field would make old records unreadable, an unreadable run with a live worker keeps its repository busy (core/src/runs/scan.ts:68-93), old workers keep rewriting run.json in the old shape (core/src/worker/run-loop.ts:168), and driver.json pins an absolute module path the worker imports after startup (core/src/worker/spawn.ts:157). A test starts a 3.0 core on a state directory holding finished and active 2.0 runs.

A run that is waiting for its operator has a stated time rule: the question has its own time limit of 12 hours, configurable for less; the run's deadline pauses while the question is pending; and when the limit passes the run ends in a state that says the question went unanswered, not in a plain 'timed_out'.

Today the deadline is absolute and keeps running, so a waiting run would become 'timed_out' (core/src/worker/run-loop.ts:241-253), and both harnesses run with allow-all permissions and never ask (core/src/harness/claude-code/agent.ts:26, core/src/harness/opencode/client.ts:82). The probe that c7 depends on must show a harness asking and waiting before this is planned.

Broker publishing is done by the core, which follows each run's log and keeps on disk how far it has published per run. After a restart it publishes what it missed, with the same event ids, and workers never connect to the broker.

The worker holds the append while it lives and the core appends only the orphan 'unknown' (core/src/worker/run-loop.ts:138-151, core/src/store/run-store.ts:62-72), so 'publish after append' needs a follower with a durable position. A test kills the core between an append and its publish and sees the event published once after restart.

Finished runs' directories have a retention rule and the cost of submit, list and attach does not grow with the number of past runs: the core does not re-read and re-validate every event of every run on each call.

Today nothing deletes run directories or rotates events.jsonl and worker.log, every submit, list and agents call parses and validates every event of every run (twice per submit; core/src/runs/scan.ts:96-107, core/src/runs/service.ts:119-123), and each attach polls every 20 milliseconds (service.ts:213). A test seeds 1,000 finished runs and a submit still returns in under 2 seconds.

tasks.summary: Probe: can each harness ask its operator a question and wait, without allow-all
acceptance_criteria: spikes/d2-approvals/ holds a runnable probe per harness (Claude Code through the AI SDK adapter, OpenCode v2 through its server API) that tries to raise one question, hold the turn, and deliver one answer into the same turn
docs/d2/probe-approvals.md records, per harness, one of: works (with the call used), does not work (with the error), or NOT VERIFIED (with the reason); no result is written without a run behind it
The record states what the capability report must say for each harness, and what part of issue 2 Decision 1 this settles
tasks.instruction: Probe code only, under spikes/, never built or linted. Never hard-timeout a local-model run; let it finish or continue the session. This task gates the operator-question tasks: if a harness cannot ask, that harness reports the capability as unsupported and the plan does not change.

tasks.summary: Rename the example node from spark to thor in fixtures, tests and documents
acceptance_criteria: No tracked file outside CHANGELOG.md history, spikes/, vendored skills and .devague/ uses spark as a node name; contract fixtures, core tests, Python tests and documents use thor
A new check in scripts/ (run by the CI lint job) fails when a tracked file names a node other than the example node in a run id, agent id or node field; it has tests for a passing and a failing file
npm test in core/ and uv run pytest -n auto pass after the rename with no test deleted
tasks.instruction: Mechanical rename first, alone in its wave, because it touches most fixtures. culture.yaml and the mesh resident's own identity are not example data: list every file you leave unchanged and why. Do not add any real host name or address anywhere.

tasks.summary: Contract 3.0: schemas, fixtures and generated types for every D2 part one change
acceptance_criteria: contract/version.json and api.json say 3.0; a core test and a CLI test prove a 2.0 client against a 3.0 core is refused with exit 2 and a message naming both versions

The schemas gain, with one fixture each: the submitter and base commit on a run, the idempotency conflict error, the typed limit error naming the limit, the question and answer events and the answer action, the terminal state for an unanswered question, retry-shortly for a control request during reattach, and limits plus active count plus per-signal admission state in the capability report
npm run check:contract-types passes, no AI SDK type appears in contract/ or core/src/contract/generated, and contract/README.md lists every breaking change from 2.0
Existing D1 guarantees keep their tests: unsupported error names the capability, the cursor is per run and gapless, a terminal state is final, unknown is never success
tasks.instruction: Schemas first, then npm run gen:contract; never hand-copy a shape. Only add what part one needs plus the fields part two reads (submitter). Part two's own shapes (members, unreachable view, bundle fetch) come with their tasks as 3.x minor additions; say so in contract/README.md.

tasks.summary: Run store: schema version, reading 2.0 run directories, startup cleanup
acceptance_criteria: Every run directory written by 3.0 carries a store schema version; a test loads a directory written by the 2.0 code (a committed fixture directory) and the run is listed with its true state
A run directory the core cannot fully read is listed as unreadable with its id, never dropped, never counted as active for a limit, and its worker is never signalled
At startup, run directories without a first event and leftover temporary files are removed, and a test proves a directory with one event is kept
docs/d2/upgrade.md states the upgrade procedure: whether active 2.0 workers must finish first and what a 3.0 core does when they have not
tasks.instruction: Files: core/src/store/. The 2.0 fixture directory is produced by running the 0.15.x core once with the stub driver and committing the result under core/test/store/fixtures/.

tasks.summary: Run store: retention of finished run directories and constant-cost reads
acceptance_criteria: A test with 500 finished runs on disk shows submit, list and attach for a new run do not read the event logs of the finished runs (count file opens through an injected reader)
A finished run directory is removed only after a stated, configurable retention period and never while its sandbox is retained or its state is unknown; the rule is in contract/README.md
A summary kept per run is rebuilt from the event log when missing or stale, and a test deletes it and gets the same listing
tasks.instruction: Files: core/src/store/. The event log stays the source of truth; any index is a cache that can be thrown away.

tasks.summary: Idempotent submit, steer and cancel with an on-disk key index and crash-safe submit order
acceptance_criteria: The key and a digest of the request are on disk before the submit is acknowledged; the same key and request returns the first run id and creates nothing; the same key with a different request returns conflict; both hold after a core restart
Steer and cancel deduplicate on their keys the same way, proven by sending each 2 times and counting 1 effect in the event log

A test kills the submit at each of its steps (after key, after run directory, after spawn); after restart a repeat with the same key yields exactly 1 run, no worker runs unlisted, and a key whose run was never established is released
tasks.instruction: New file core/src/store/idempotency.ts plus the submit path in core/src/runs/service.ts. Order on disk: key, then run directory, then spawn. Use fault injection points, not sleeps.

tasks.summary: Record the base commit when a submit is accepted and build the sandbox from it
acceptance_criteria: The run record holds the commit resolved at accept time; a test moves the host HEAD after the submit and before the sandbox is ready, and the bundle is built from the recorded commit
A submit to a repository with no commits or an unresolvable HEAD is refused at submit with a typed error, not failed later
tasks.instruction: Files: core/src/runs/service.ts, core/src/worker/, core/src/sandbox/worktree.ts. Today the worker resolves HEAD up to 180 s after submit; move the resolution to accept time and pass the commit to the worker.

tasks.summary: Concurrent runs in one repository with operator-configured limits and no implicit limit
acceptance_criteria: With no limit configured, 3 submits to 1 repository are all accepted and each is steered independently; the busy refusal and its error are gone from code, contract and explain text
With a per-repository or per-host limit configured, a submit past it is refused at submit with the typed error naming the limit and its value; nothing is queued
A test runs 2 runs in 1 repository to completion and shows each runs branch holds only its own commits, the host checkout and index are byte-identical before and after, and no git worktree exists
The worktree_isolation capability text states what is guaranteed: a sandbox clone per run, not a host worktree
tasks.instruction: Files: core/src/runs/service.ts, core/src/harness/config.ts or a new core/src/daemon limits config, core/src/daemon/harness-catalog.ts. Limits come from the core's config file, never from a request. Run the concurrent-fetch check from the parked item here: two results fetched into one repository at the same moment.

tasks.summary: Reattach to surviving workers after a core restart, before answering control requests
acceptance_criteria: After a core restart with 2 live workers, steer, cancel and attach each take effect on the right run; the reconnect capability is reported as supported
A control request that arrives before a run's reattach attempt has finished waits or gets retry-shortly, never live control unavailable; a test holds the reattach open to prove it
A worker whose control socket does not answer is reported unknown and receives no signal; controls of terminal runs are not rebuilt

Killing the core with SIGKILL sends no signal to any worker, and a worker with the core absent still enforces its deadline and writes its terminal event; the per-run control socket protocol is unchanged (existing protocol tests untouched)
tasks.instruction: Files: core/src/runs/ (reconcile path, control.ts), core/src/worker/spawn.ts reconnectWorker (today only tests call it). Also examine the parked question: can a dying core finish asynchronous work after it releases the state-directory lock and overlap a new core's reattach; write the finding in docs/d2/.

acceptance_criteria: A cancel whose grace period ends during retention cleanup leaves a retention record, proven by a test that delays cleanup past the grace period
The worker's conflict reply on a refused append has a test

risks.text: What makes two checkouts the same repository across hosts, and which commit a remote run starts from when the hosts' checkouts differ, is not decided. The owner said a repository can exist on more than one host. The part two design record must answer it before the remote submit task.
How a core announces itself is not chosen. The broker is loopback-only and anonymous today, and membership must not travel over the chat mesh, so neither existing channel fits as it is.

The approvals probe may show that one or both harnesses cannot ask a question without allow-all. Then that harness reports the capability as unsupported and the operator-question path is proven on the stub driver only.

A dying core may finish asynchronous work after releasing the state-directory lock and overlap a new core's reattach to the same worker. Examined in the reattach task; a real overlap would need a fencing rule not in this plan.
git's behaviour when two results are fetched into one repository at the same moment while refs are packed was not determined. Checked in the concurrency task.
The heat signal's format and location were not re-read for this plan. The capability task reads the publisher first and reports unknown if it cannot.

Part two acceptance needs at least 2 real hosts set up by the owner. Every probe so far ran on x86_64; the run image is single-architecture, so an ARM host (the Jetson Thor of the examples) may report its harnesses as unavailable.
The gateway admit signal depends on lobes-cli issue 346 being merged and released. D2 ships without it; until then harnesses that use the gateway are admitted on harness, limit and heat only.
How the core daemon is supervised (a systemd user unit, or started by the CLI) is undecided and not in this plan. Reattach makes a restart safe but nothing restarts the core.
Rollback from 3.0 to 2.0 after a 3.0 core has written run records is not planned and not tested.
OpenShell is alpha and pinned; a change in its CLI or SDK can break sandbox handling in any task that touches it.
Not covered by this plan: a test that a retained sandbox is deleted after its 7 days, and the OpenCode retention path.

Found by dispatching through agents on 2026-11-26: when a harness reads a repository file containing the OpenShell credential placeholder text, the gateway's egress proxy refuses the next model request (provider.auth: a credential placeholder in the request body cannot be forwarded) and the run fails. Five tracked files here contain it. Any repository text with that marker can end a run; not handled by any D2 task.

Found the same way: a run whose turn fails collects nothing. Ten minutes of an agent's work, including any commits it made in the sandbox, was lost with the sandbox. D1 keeps the sandbox only when the turn completed and collection failed.
